GroCliq AI · 2026

Helping small teams hand marketing work to AI they can trust

I mapped where AI tools fail small businesses, then designed a workspace where five specialist AI employees share one brand memory and every output waits for human approval.

See screens
RoleSole UI/UX designer
Timeline2026, MVP designed in two months
TeamFounders and developers
PlatformDesktop-first web app
The 30-second version
The problem

Small teams juggle several AI and marketing tools, re-explain their brand every time, and can’t tell what the AI wrote from what a person changed.

What I did

As the sole designer, I read the market and the founders’ knowledge, then designed a workspace of five specialist AI employees that share one Brand DNA, with approval before anything goes live. I designed the MVP in two months.

What I learned

The need was trust more than efficiency. I had no end-user interviews, so the personas are assumptions still to test.

Overview

Turning scattered AI tools into one workspace

The company needed an internal workspace where several AI employees could work together across content, SEO, creative generation and workflows. Existing tools were fragmented, so people switched between platforms and managed repetitive steps by hand.

It was a 0→1 product with nothing internal to reference. I ran the research, defined the scope with the founders, designed the information architecture, the AI employees and a design system, then designed the screens and worked with developers through implementation.

5

AI employees designed, each with a role and identity

3

competitors analysed in depth

5

insight clusters from affinity mapping

180+

screens designed

Empathise→Define→Ideate→Prototype
Credit. I was the sole designer. Scope and priorities were set with the founding team, and I say below where a decision was shared.
Problem

People end up managing AI tools instead of delegating to them

Small teams already use ChatGPT, Canva, SEO tools and freelancers side by side. Each AI session starts from zero, so people re-explain their brand, switch tools to finish one job and check every output by hand. Approvals and publishing happen outside the product, so nobody can tell what the AI wrote and what a person changed.

4–7

tools switched between in a day, noted in the workflow-fragmentation cluster (qualitative)

4

recurring pain points in competitor reviews and community threads

3

more from founder and stakeholder discussions

0

end-user interviews; access was limited before launch

Research question. How might we help a lean team feel like they have a full marketing department?
Research

Reading the market when users weren’t available

The product was pre-launch, so I couldn’t sit down with end users. I leaned on structured founder discussions, competitor teardowns and public reviews, and treated each as evidence rather than opinion.

Desk research

Landscape review

AI workforce tools, automation platforms and marketing SaaS: positioning, features and UX patterns.

Stakeholder

Founder discussions

Documented and synthesised. Founders carry accumulated exposure to customer conversations.

Secondary

Reviews and community

Product Hunt, forums and user discussions. A point repeated across sources became a high-confidence priority.

Synthesis

Affinity mapping

Observations became insight cards, grouped into recurring themes.

My read of the market at the time. The last column is what the product set out to cover, not a measured result.

The gap that mattered for design wasn’t one feature. It was a team of specialists that share context in one place.

SWOT as a design constraint

I used SWOT to spot design risks early, not as a business exercise.

Strengths
  • Five deeply specialised agents rather than generalist bots
  • Only platform with rank tracking plus SEO audit
  • A shared Business DNA memory layer
Weaknesses
  • Desktop-only at launch
  • Onboarding complexity: five agents, DNA setup and a workflow builder
  • Low brand awareness
Opportunities
  • GEO and local SEO writing are underserved
  • A mobile companion for monitoring and approvals
  • An agency tier with multiple workspaces
Threats
  • Sintra expanding its agent depth
  • Marblism closing the coordination gap
  • Tool fatigue and churn if ROI isn’t clear in 30 days

Pain points, from two kinds of source

Reviews and community
  • Context loss between sessions. Brand guidelines re-explained every time.
  • Unclear output ownership. AI work and human edits blur together.
  • Generic outputs. No contextual brand understanding.
  • Tool fragmentation. Several tools for one workflow.
Founder discussions
  • Managing tools instead of delegating. Coordination replaces real work.
  • No central brand knowledge. Outputs lack consistency.
  • Disconnected approvals. Publishing happens outside the product.

Two proto-personas

These are working assumptions built from founder knowledge, review language and inferred behaviour. They are not real people.

Proto-persona

The scaling founder

Aryan Mehta, 32. Early-stage e-commerce, team of 3–10, using ChatGPT, Canva, freelancers and SEO tools. Wants to scale marketing without a large team. Struggles with repeating brand guidelines, generic output and low trust in AI work.

Proto-persona

The overwhelmed marketing manager

Sarah Lee, 29. SMB with 20–100 employees, covering SEO, social, email and some support. Wants more content with fewer resources. Struggles with inconsistent quality and little time to learn another tool.

Affinity map: five clusters

Context and memory, role clarity and trust, output accountability, workflow fragmentation, and adoption anxiety. Built from synthesised inputs, not interview transcripts.

What I learned

01

It was trust, not only efficiency

Founders needed AI that felt like delegation, not another tool to supervise.

02

It was bandwidth, not capability

Managers needed systems that cut cognitive load while making output more reliable.

03

Behind the frustration was a fear of falling behind

People worried about competitors using AI better. The product had to feel empowering rather than intimidating, which shaped onboarding, the AI identities and the interaction patterns.

My first assumption was wrong. The obvious framing was efficiency. The founder synthesis pointed to trust, so approval and transparency became design drivers, not extras.
Limits. No end-user interviews. Personas, empathy maps and the affinity map come from founder knowledge, competitor reviews and inferred workflows. They are assumptions to validate with real users.
Ideation

Five decisions that shaped the product

For each product area I framed a How might we question, sketched against the requirements, and took concepts to the founding team for reaction. The aim was to fail cheaply and early, before committing to wireframes.

Five questions to answer

Efficiency

Help a lean team feel like a full department

How might we help a lean team feel like they have a full marketing department?

Identity

Specialists, not chatbots

How might we make AI agents feel like specialists rather than generic chatbots?

Memory

Never start from zero

How might we preserve brand knowledge so AI never starts from zero?

Transparency

Confidence and control

How might we give users confidence and control over AI-generated outputs?

Scalability

From one agent to five

How might we design a workspace that scales from one agent to five without overwhelming users?

Requirements I tested every decision against

FunctionalDesign
Specialised AI agents. Five agents with clearly different capabilities.Agent clarity. Always clear which agent you’re talking to.
Persistent brand memory. Shared across agents and sessions.Low-friction delegation. Assign a task in under three interactions.
Approval workflows. Review checkpoints before anything goes live.Persistent context. Brand memory and history stay in reach.
Centralised management. One place for tasks, inbox and notifications.Calm authority. Capable without being overwhelming.

Three principles

Principle

Specialists, not tools

Each employee has its own identity, capability, tone and workflow.

Principle

Human in the loop, always

AI actions are built around review, approval and checkpoints, not blind automation.

Principle

The system knows you

Brand knowledge, preferences and history stay accessible, so people never feel they’re starting from zero.

Decisions I made

Five specialists, not one assistant

Considered
One general assistant, or a generic AI interface with a label attached.
Chose
Five employees, each with a role, tone, colour and character, so people pick a teammate for the job.
Gave up
A single entry point. The SWOT flagged a steeper learning curve for first-time AI users.

Approval before publishing

Considered
Letting agents publish automatically.
Chose
Review, approve and schedule checkpoints in the Inbox, so people keep control of critical decisions.
Gave up
Some speed. Content waits for a person before it goes live.

One Brand DNA for every agent

Considered
Re-uploading brand guidelines in each chat, as users did with other tools.
Chose
A DNA module for company information, tone and voice, and knowledge sources, shared by all employees.
Gave up
A setup step before first use. DNA setup comes before the first brief in the onboarding story.

MVP scope with the founders

Considered
Launching every automation at once.
Chose
An MVP of the unified Inbox with approvals, agent chat, the DNA module, a home dashboard, and the agent identity system with its design foundations.
Gave up
Cross-agent analytics, multi-channel publishing and image and video production were scheduled after the MVP.

Desktop first

Considered
A mobile companion for monitoring and approvals.
Chose
A desktop-first MVP within the two-month window.
Gave up
Managing the AI team on the go, which the SWOT lists as a real friction point for founders who work across devices.
Dashboard→Choose employee→Prompt→Generate→Review→Approve→Schedule or publish

Storyboards: two moments to design for

1. The solo founder at the end of the day.

2. Onboarding a new business.

Both stories end in the same place: output that already sounds like the brand.

Prioritisation with the founders

MVP

High impact, lower effort

  • Unified Inbox with approval workflows
  • Agent chat for briefing and output generation
  • DNA module for brand knowledge
  • Home dashboard
  • Agent identity system and design foundations
Post-MVP

High impact, higher effort

  • Cross-agent analytics and performance tracking
  • Multi-channel publishing integrations
  • AI image and video production (Mo)
Shared decision. Scope was set on an effort-versus-impact matrix with the founding team. With two months, the design work focused on the MVP.

Value proposition

The owner’s fears, losing creative control and publishing mistakes, are why approval sits before publishing.

Task flows

Content creation

DNA setup

Both flows return to a review step instead of dead-ending, so a rejected draft or incomplete setup is one step from fixed.

Information architecture

Home, Inbox, DNA and Settings at the top. Each employee has chat, a working surface, powerups and guidelines.

Low-fidelity wireframes

Over 100 low-fidelity screens in total. I used them to test navigation before any visual design.

Designs

A calm workspace run by a team of specialists

The brand had four attributes: collaborative, intelligent, efficient and approachable. Instead of one assistant, people meet a team, each with a role, a personality and a colour.

Lessons

Evaluation and what I’d do next

Honest scope. This case study doesn’t include usability testing with end users. Decisions rest on founder knowledge, competitor reviews and proto-personas, and the measures below are planned, not measured.

Problem to solution

Research findingIn the product
Context lost between sessionsBrand DNA module and persistent context shared by every employee
Generic outputsBrand-aware generation, plus style questions each specialist asks up front
Disconnected approvalsApprovals and ideas in the Inbox, with publish and schedule actions on the output
Tool fragmentationChat, Inbox, DNA and workflows in one navigation
Fear of AI and falling behindNamed, friendly specialists and onboarding that starts with Brand DNA (not yet validated)
Unclear ownership of AI versus human editsNot yet solved: version history and an audit trail are future work
Managing the team on the goNot yet designed: a mobile companion is future work

What I’d measure

Outcome

Brief to scheduled post

Planned. How long a founder takes from prompt to scheduled content.

Task

Delegation effort

Planned. Can people assign a task in under three interactions?

Confidence

Trust in outputs

Planned. How often outputs are approved without regeneration.

Recovery

Fixing a bad output

Planned. How quickly someone regenerates or edits and moves on.

If I had more time

  • Run moderated tests with five small-business owners on the founder storyboard flow.
  • Replace the proto-personas with findings from real interviews.
  • Design version history and an audit trail for AI versus human edits.
  • Design the mobile companion for approvals and monitoring.
  • Document one inconsistent screen before and after the design system.

Designing a system, not screens

Designing this workspace taught me to think beyond single screens. From information architecture to reusable components and working with developers, I saw how design decisions scale into a real product. It was my first chance to design a large AI workspace from zero, and it showed me that the real work was reducing complexity so people could delegate with confidence.

Pinpo AI · 2026

Design feedback that flies to the exact spot

I built a desktop buddy that looks at the Figma frame you’ve selected, asks Gemini for a short critique, then flies to each problem and says what’s wrong and how to fix it. I scored the first version over 13 test runs, then redesigned it after reviewing my own renders, and report what held up and what didn’t.

RoleProduct designer and builder
TimelineOctober to November 2026, v1 scored, v2 polished
TeamSolo
PlatformWindows desktop app (Electron)
The 30-second version
The problem

Design feedback arrives as a paragraph, and the designer has to map each sentence back onto the canvas.

What I did

I built a Windows buddy that reads the selected Figma frame, asks Gemini for one to four findings, and flies to each one with a ring, a short explanation and a one-line fix. After scoring v1 I redesigned it as v2, because the buddy was covering the design it was critiquing.

What I learned

In v1, pointing worked (all 31 ratings landed on the right element) and the wait didn’t (40.8 seconds on average against a 6-second bar). A critic must never hide what it critiques. I haven’t scored v2.

Overview

From a screenshot to a guided tour of what to fix

Press a hotkey, type a request like “roast this”, and a character I drew flies over the selected frame, drops a ring on one element and explains it in a card. Then it moves to the next finding.

It is a working prototype, not a launched product. I designed the interaction and the buddy, wrote the critique rules, built the Electron app and added a small scorecard so I could test it honestly.

Then I reviewed v1’s on-screen renders and ran a second pass. v2 moves the buddy off the frame, rebuilds the card around severity, and adds a command bar with quick chips, a tour summary with copy all, a “why it matters” line, a first-run intro and tray settings.

31

v1 findings rated across 13 test runs (4 more went unrated)

30

rated right element and right explanation

13/13

first findings landed on the right element

40.8s

v1 average wait to the first finding, against a 6s bar

Hotkey→Command→Screenshot→Find frame→Gemini→Tour
Credit. Solo project. Gemini supplies the critique; the design work is everything around it: the interaction, the prompt rules, the buddy, the tour and the test. Numbers on this page are self-rated by one tester, me, and all of them are from v1. I haven’t re-scored v2.
Problem

A critique is only useful if you can find what it’s talking about

This is how I framed the problem, not something I measured. When feedback arrives as a paragraph, the designer has to map each sentence back onto the canvas, and a long answer can bury the one thing that matters. I wanted feedback short enough to read mid-flow and tied to one element.

1–4

findings per critique, most severe first (a rule in the prompt)

1

specific element per finding, with its own bounding box

≤6

words in a title (fix: 12 words, explanation: 20)

14

design principles named in the prompt, 7 UI and 7 UX

Research question. How might we give a designer feedback that points at one exact element, explains it in a sentence and is honest about how sure it is?
Research

No user interviews: a build, a rubric and a scored test

Pinpo started as a tool for myself, so I didn’t run user research. My evidence is the product doc I wrote, an earlier Figma-plugin attempt, a scored test of v1 and, for v2, a review of my own renders. I say where that falls short.

Product doc

Feature list v0.1

Critic and Guide modes, a Normal and a Gen Z tone, and a generic UI/UX rubric first, with no setup.

Earlier build

A Figma plugin

A “Critique selection” button sent the selected frame to Gemini and printed the reply in a sidebar. I tested it on one Login frame, then parked it for a desktop app.

Rubric

14 principles

Seven UI (hierarchy, contrast, typography, spacing, alignment, consistency, colour) and seven UX (primary action, next step, labels, tap targets, feedback and states, cognitive load, accessibility basics).

Test

Scorecard hotkeys

While a finding is on screen I press one key to rate it. Every press writes a row to a CSV, which I recompute the numbers from.

Audit: what the feature list promised vs what the app does (after v2)

FeatureStatusWhat the code does
Critic modeBuiltOne critique mode. “Roast this” is just the typed command.
Guide modeNot builtNo code for it yet.
Normal and Gen Z tonePartlyTyping “roast” switches the thinking messages (“Cracking my knuckles…”). The critique prompt is the same for every command.
UI/UX rubric, no setupBuilt14 principles in the prompt. No brief needed.
Project brief, design-system profileNot builtPlanned after v1.
Find the selected frameBuilt, Figma onlyReads Figma’s blue outline and corner handles from pixels, with no plugin. If it can’t find one it asks you to select a frame.
Point, then walk through findingsBuiltRing, link line and card, then ← → and Esc.
Screens and systemsLimitedPrimary display only. Tested on Windows only.
“Nothing is saved”Not true yetDebug code (scorecard hotkeys, a demo flight and debug screenshots in the temp folder) is still in the main process, and settings now save to a file in the app-data folder. Remove the debug code before a public build.
Tour summary and copy allBuilt in v2Right on the last finding opens a summary, and C copies every finding as plain text. Tours with one finding skip it.
“Why it matters”Built in v2W opens one sentence on what the person using the screen feels or misses. If Gemini skips the field, the block and its hint don’t appear.
First-run intro, tray settingsBuilt in v2Three buddy messages, and a tray menu with card theme, replay intro, send buddy home and quit.
Dismiss or save a findingNot builtOn the original list. Not built yet.

How I scored v1

Ctrl+Alt+1

Right

Pointed at the right element and the explanation holds.

Ctrl+Alt+3

Wrong explanation

Right element, but what it says is wrong.

Ctrl+Alt+2

Missed

Pointed at the wrong element. None in the log.

I set two v1 bars: finding 1 lands on the right element in at least 8 of 10 screens, and the first finding arrives within 6 seconds of pressing Enter.

Every first finding landed on the right element (13 of 13), past the 8-of-10 bar. Speed is a different story.

Seconds from Enter to the first finding, in order. Grey is the 10 October run from an earlier build. The dashed line is the 6-second bar. The number at the end of each bar is the Gemini Flash version that answered.

Only 1 of 13 runs beat 6 seconds. Waiting for Gemini is 98% of the delay; the app’s own work adds about half a second. Runs 2 to 7 averaged about 63s and runs 8 to 13 about 21s, ending 15.3s, 8.6s and 4.2s. The log doesn’t record what changed, so I can’t say why.

What it points out most

Contrast and readability13
Typography3
Clear primary action3
Labels and copy3
Visual hierarchy3
Five other principles6

Findings by principle, out of 31. Severity split: 10 high, 15 medium, 6 low.

What I learned

01

Pointing wasn’t the hard part

All 31 ratings landed on the right element. The weak spot is the wait, not the aim.

02

It reaches for contrast first

13 of 31 findings were contrast, out of 14 principles. My scorecard can’t tell me which problems it missed.

03

A wrong explanation is the risk that matters

The one miss was a spacing claim (“cramped above keyboard”) on the right element. The prompt tells the model to check spacing, overlap and position claims before including them, so that rule is worth keeping and testing.

Limits. One rater who also built the tool, judging by eye. 31 ratings over 13 runs, with 4 findings left unrated. No “missed problem” metric. One Windows machine, and frames from several Figma files rather than a controlled set. Answers came from three Gemini Flash versions. v2 has not been scored. It was checked for syntax and layout logic, then tried on screen in Figma through screenshots.
Ideation

Fourteen decisions that shaped Pinpo

The first six follow from the problem above. The next eight follow from reviewing v1’s renders. Each has a cost.

Three principles

Principle

Point, don’t just describe

Every finding is tied to one element on the canvas.

Principle

Never in the way

The overlay is click-through and never takes focus. It grabs the arrow keys, Esc, C and W only while a tour, summary or intro is showing. Since v2 it also stays off the design.

Principle

Say how sure you are

Each finding is Sure or Possible, and the model is told to drop claims it can’t verify. Since v2 only “Possible” is shown.

Decisions I made

A desktop buddy, not a Figma plugin

Considered
The plugin I’d built, with the reply in a sidebar.
Chose
A screen overlay with a hotkey, a typed command and a character that flies to the spot.
Gave up
Access to Figma’s real file structure. Pinpo only sees pixels, and runs on Windows.

Find the frame from pixels

Considered
Sending the whole screen, which includes Figma’s own panels.
Chose
Look for Figma’s blue outline and white corner handles, then crop to that frame.
Gave up
Working anywhere. With no frame selected it asks you to click one, and it ignores hover outlines.

One exact element per finding

Considered
A paragraph of notes about the frame.
Chose
Gemini returns a bounding box for one element and the ring lands at its centre.
Gave up
Outlining the whole box. A wide element gets a single point.

A tour, one finding at a time

Considered
Pinning every finding on the frame at once.
Chose
Most severe first, with → for next, ← for back and Esc to close.
Gave up
An overview at a glance, which the v2 summary card now gives at the end. Opening the command bar also ends a tour, because typing needs the arrow keys.

Say how sure the model is

Considered
Presenting every finding as fact.
Chose
A Sure or Possible flag, and a prompt rule to drop spacing, overlap or text claims it can’t verify.
Gave up
Some findings. Unverifiable ones are dropped and “possible” ones carry a caveat.

Keep going when a model fails

Considered
One fixed model.
Chose
Ask Google which Flash models the key can use, try the newest first, retry on busy or slow, time out at 15 seconds and show a plain-language error.
Gave up
Consistency. In my log gemini-3.6-flash answered 10 runs, 3.5 answered 2 and 3.7 answered 1.

What my own review of v1 found

I reviewed v1’s renders and it still felt like a prototype, for five reasons:

  • The buddy covered the design it was critiquing, the worst failure for a design critic.
  • The card had weak hierarchy: severity was a small dot, “Sure” floated alone and key hints never went away.
  • The command bar was the plainest part, with a hint that was unreadable on Figma’s light grey canvas.
  • Spacing, type and colour were inconsistent between the bar, card and pill.
  • It lacked what makes a tool feel finished: a wrap-up, a way to export findings, the reasoning, onboarding and settings.

I worked in that order, biggest visible effect first.

Decisions I made in v2

The buddy stands beside the frame

Before
The buddy landed on the headline and hovered over the Continue button.
Chose
A layout planner puts the buddy just outside the frame, level with the target, and the card on the opposite side. If there is no room left and right it goes above or below. If the frame fills the screen it falls back to the old behaviour.
Why
The critic must never hide the thing being critiqued.
Trade-off
In a tight row of frames the buddy ends up on a neighbouring frame, never the one being critiqued.

Severity first, and “Sure” stays silent

Before
Severity was a small dot and “Sure” floated alone.
Chose
A filled severity badge in the header and a matching colour bar on the card’s top edge. The ring, link line and summary dots take the same colour. Only “Possible” shows, as a dashed pill.
Why
Severity is the first thing a reader wants to know, and “Sure” read like a leftover label. Show the exception, not the default.

Key hints that fade with use

Before
Key hints never went away.
Chose
Full hints for the first 3 tours, one faded key for tours 4 to 8, then none. The count is kept in local storage.
Why
Hints are useful once and noise after that.

The reasoning, on demand

Before
The card said what was wrong, not what it costs the person using the screen.
Chose
Gemini returns a one-sentence “why” of at most 25 words. W opens it as a “Why it matters” block under the fix.
Why
It is what makes a critique persuasive, and hidden by default so the card stays short.
Trade-off
About 25 more output tokens per finding, so a small latency increase.

A wrap-up and copy all

Before
A tour was linear and ephemeral.
Chose
Right on the last finding opens a summary: a count, a chip per severity and a row per finding. C copies every finding as plain text. Tours with one finding skip it.
Why
It gets the findings into a ticket, a message or a case study.

A command bar that teaches

Before
A plain box, with a near-white hint that was unreadable on Figma’s light grey canvas.
Chose
A Pinpo icon, a focus glow, an Enter key hint, three chips that send immediately (roast this, check spacing, critique) and a hint on its own dark pill. The bar window grew from 64px to 156px tall.
Why
The bar is the first thing people see, and the chips teach the three most useful commands.

An intro and a tray icon

Before
A background app with no window had no visible home and no way to change its behaviour.
Chose
A first-run intro of three buddy messages, and a tray icon with a menu: Ask Pinpo, card theme, replay intro, send buddy home and quit. Settings are saved to a file.
Why
The intro teaches three things: select a frame, press the hotkey, use the arrow keys.
Lesson
The first intro auto-advanced every 6 seconds, so I couldn’t screenshot it. It is now keyboard-driven.

Grab keys only when needed

Before
A replay hotkey on Ctrl+Alt+I collided with Figma’s DevTools shortcut.
Chose
Remove it in favour of an “intro” command. Arrow keys, Esc, C and W are registered only while a tour, summary or intro is active, so C is grabbed only while the summary shows.
Why
Any global key has to be checked against Figma’s own. Figma keeps its comment shortcut the rest of the time.
Hotkey→Command→Screenshot→Frame→Gemini→Findings→Tour

Flows

One critique

Reading the findings

Where does the ring land? Three coordinate spaces

SpaceUnitUsed for
OverlayCSS pixels (DIPs)Where the buddy, ring and card are drawn
ScreenshotReal pixels (DIPs × scale factor)Frame detection and the crop
Gemini box0 to 1000, [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax]Normalised over the cropped frame, so it needs no scale factor

The ring sits at the box’s centre, mapped into the frame’s DIP rectangle. My rule from the notes: convert at the screenshot boundary, once.

Designs

A small character that flies to the problem

Pinpo is a violet-blue buddy I drew in Figma. It idles, flies on a spring so it overshoots slightly, drops a pulsing ring on the target and puts a hand to its chin while it thinks. The card is light by default so it reads over Figma’s dark canvas. Dark, and the opposite of the screen, are in the tray menu.

Brand

#7E95F3Buddy light
#9D97FACard light
#F4F3FDCard dark
#1B1B27
High
#E5484DMedium
#E08A00Low

Anatomy of a finding card, v1 and v2

  • Lens and principle. UI or UX, then the one principle it breaks. Long names truncate.
  • Severity. A filled badge in the header and a matching colour bar along the top edge. High, medium or low, most severe first.
  • Title and explanation. A title of up to six words and one sentence of up to 20.
  • Fix. One line of up to 12 words, in its own box.
  • Why it matters. Opens with W. One sentence of up to 25 words.
  • Progress and keys. Position in the tour, with hints that fade. A “Possible” finding adds a dashed pill in the header.

v2 uses one scale across the bar, card, pill and toast. Spacing is 4, 8, 12 and 16 px, radii are 18 px for the card and 12 px for inner blocks, and type is 11.5, 13, 14 and 15.5 px.

1. Waiting

Speed is the unsolved problem, so the waiting state does extra work. In v2 the status pill grows away from the frame.

2. Pointing and explaining

A ring marks the element, a thin line links it to the card, and the fix sits in its own box. This answers the “find what it’s talking about” problem. In v2 the ring, link line and badge share the severity colour, and the buddy and card flank the frame.

3. When it can’t, or gets it wrong

The v1 stills are crops of real screenshots from 27 October, taken over Figma frames from several of my files. The v2 stills are screenshots from 7 November over frames in a Figma test file.

4. Wrapping up

Tours with one finding skip the summary. C is only grabbed while the summary shows, so Figma keeps its comment shortcut.

5. Command bar and first run

The intro plays once and is keyboard-driven. Type “intro” in the command bar, or use the tray menu, to replay it.

Lessons

What held up, what didn’t, what’s next

Problem to solution

Problem I framedIn PinpoEvidence so far
Feedback you have to find on the canvasRing, link line and card on one element31 of 31 ratings pointed at the right element
Long answers1–4 findings, short explanation, one fix linePrompt rules. Not yet tested for readability
TrustSure or Possible flag, and a check-before-claiming rule1 wrong explanation in 31 (v1). The “Why it matters” line is new and not yet checked
WaitingThinking pose beside the frame, status lines, a slow messagev1: mean 40.8s and 1 of 13 under 6s. Not solved. v2 not re-timed, and the “why” line adds a little output
Fragile modelsTry the next model, plain-language errorsgemini-3.5-flash answered 2 of 13 runs
The buddy hid the design it was critiquingBuddy and card flank the frame, placed by a layout plannerChecked in on-screen renders only. Not scored
A card that was hard to scanSeverity badge and colour, “Possible” only, fading key hintsSeen in renders. Not tested with other designers
A critique with no reasoning and no wrap-up“Why it matters” on W, a summary card and copy allNot yet tested with other designers

What I’d measure next (planned, not yet measured)

Speed

Time to first finding

Under 6 seconds, with the wait broken down by step.

Coverage

Missed problems

List the real problems on a frame first, then count what Pinpo misses.

Raters

Other designers

3 to 5 designers rate the same findings, so it isn’t only my judgement.

Consistency

Same frame, repeated

Run one frame several times and compare the findings.

Version

Re-score v2

Run the same scorecard on v2, from a clean install, and compare it with v1.

If I had more time

  • Find where the wait goes, and show the first finding while the rest is still being written.
  • Build Guide mode and a real Normal and Gen Z switch in the prompt, not only in the status lines.
  • Add the project brief and a design-system profile, so UX findings have a goal behind them.
  • Remove the debug code from the main process (scorecard hotkeys, demo flight, debug screenshots) and move the API key out of config.local.json into proper setup.
  • Support other tools and more than one monitor, and test on another operating system.
  • Build “dismiss or save a finding”, which was on the original list.
  • Do a full pass on a clean install: the first-run intro, the tray theme switch and a full tour with W and C.

Pointing was the easy half

Making the buddy land on the right element worked from the first test. The design work that’s left is making the wait feel acceptable and every claim trustworthy enough that a designer acts on it. v2 added a second lesson: a design critic must never hide the design it is critiquing, which I only saw by reviewing my own renders.

Helping first-time applicants know what to do before they apply

I researched why people get stuck on Indian government paperwork, then designed a goal-first guide that turns a vague need into a case-specific checklist and a clear next step.

RoleUX Researcher & Designer
Timeline2026
TeamSolo project
PlatformMobile app
The 30-second version
The problem

People know their goal but not which documents apply, which office to go to or what happens next, so they lose days and trips.

What I did

I interviewed 7 applicants, found 4 friction themes, and designed a goal-first guide: three short questions, then a checklist for their case. 27 high-fidelity screens.

What I learned

The problem is ambiguity, not too many portals. I haven’t usability-tested the screens yet.

Overview

Making a confusing system feel like a first step

India’s documents and certificates are handled across central, state and municipal authorities. People often know their goal, like “a domicile certificate for my daughter’s admission”, but not which documents apply, which office handles it, or what happens next.

Pehla Kadam (“first step”) starts from that goal, asks three short questions, and returns a verified, case-specific path before the person starts the application.

7

applicants interviewed about a real, recent application

4

friction themes found across different documents

9

features, each traced to a research finding

27

high-fidelity screens designed

Problem

Knowing the goal isn’t the same as knowing the path

Government systems often expect people to know what they’re looking for before they begin. First-timers visit the wrong office, carry the wrong documents, get redirected, or pay agents to figure it out. A wrong assumption costs a day, a trip, or money.

3

trips in ~2 weeks, one to the wrong office (R6)

20+

days an Aadhaar update sat in validation (R1)

2

visits over 10–12 days after one rejected document (R4)

45+

days for Aadhaar demographic updates in 2025, up from ~2 weeks

Research question. How might we help first-time applicants turn a vague government-document goal into a clear, situation-specific path, before they start the application?
Research

Looking beyond the portal

I combined desk research with real stories, then checked a small sample against larger public data.

Desk research

Landscape review

DigiLocker and UMANG tested on one question: where does the journey start?

Primary

WhatsApp interviews

Reached varied ages and digital confidence with no travel. Asked about the last real document, never hypotheticals.

Grouped by theme rather than by person, to separate patterns from one-offs.

Secondary

A scale check on whether friction goes beyond my sample.

“

Especially if it could tell me, ‘For your case, take these five documents.’

R4
Respondent 4Shop owner, 42 · domicile certificate

Is this only anecdotal?

DARPG’s call centre logged 1,96,214 feedback calls on state/UT services (Jan–Aug 2025). Only 91,476 were resolved.

46% resolved. This shows friction is broader than my sample; it does not prove the design solution.

What we learned

01 · The problem is ambiguity

People answered questions the system should have resolved: which document applies, which are needed, where to go, what if it goes wrong.

02 · Intermediaries sell confidence

Agents, family and CSC operators weren’t only filling forms. They reduced uncertainty about what to do next.

03 · Some users are proxies

Guidance has to be simple enough to understand, remember, explain and hand to someone else.

My first assumption was wrong. I expected the issue to be too many portals and offices. The interviews showed ambiguity: even with information in hand, people couldn’t tell what applied to them. That moved the design from “gather everything” to “resolve for this person.”
Limitation. This is a small qualitative sample, so I treat it as directional. It identifies recurring friction; it doesn’t measure how many people face it.

Lessons

Evaluation and what I’d do next

Honest scope. I haven’t usability-tested the high-fidelity screens. Decisions rest on the primary research, and the measures below are planned, not yet measured.

Problem to solution

Research findingIn the app
Compulsory vs. “if applicable” (R2, R3, R4)Three questions, then a case-specific checklist
“For your case, take these five documents” (R4)Personal checklist with accepted options per item
Wrong office, three trips (R6)Authority named upfront; apply online or at an office
Dense language, proxy applicant (R7)Plain names, short steps, an easy-to-share checklist
Validation stuck 20+ days (R1)“Action Required” state with the exact blocker
Payment deducted (R5)Not yet designed; flagged as future work

What I’d measure

Outcome

Trips to complete

R4 needed two visits over 10–12 days.

Task

Checklist accuracy

Can people name which documents apply to them, unaided?

Confidence

Pre-start certainty

Self-rated, before vs. after the flow.

Recovery

Time to resolve a blocker

From an “Action Required” state.

If I had more time

  • Run moderated tests with 3–5 first-time applicants, including a proxy, on the domicile journey.
  • Design the payment-failure state for Respondent 5’s scenario.
  • Trim signup to match “no registration or passwords required”, or reword that line.
  • Build a standalone office result with a map and directions.
  • Extend to the income certificate by adding its rules to the same flow.

Designing for clarity before action

People don’t get stuck because government processes are complex. They get stuck because no one tells them, before they start, what applies to their case. Small interface decisions mattered most: asking before answering, placing reassurance at the moment of doubt, and naming the next step.
